patient.name: Maureen Gallagher
patient.complaint: Six months of tiredness, a sore tongue and tingling in both feet
background: Vitiligo on her hands since her forties
Widowed last year; lives alone in Kilburn and eats little
Drinks 2 to 3 glasses of wine most evenings

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely cause?' with a macrocytic anaemia: neurological signs mean B12, autoimmune clues mean pernicious anaemia, and alcohol, pregnancy or poor diet without neurology mean folate.

points: Maureen, 63, **exhausted** and breathless walking to the shops.
Her **tongue is sore** and looks smooth and red.
**Pins and needles** in both feet for 2 months.

steps.lead: Tiredness with a sore tongue in an older woman: think **megaloblastic** anaemia, where the red cells are too big because DNA synthesis fails.
Maureen has **vitiligo** and **hypothyroidism**: autoimmune clues pointing to **pernicious anaemia**. Her poor diet and wine also risk **folate** deficiency.

points: Vibration sense **absent** at both ankles; reduced at the knees.
Reduced pinprick in a stocking pattern.

steps.lead: Maureen has the shared features (fatigue, pallor, glossitis) **plus** neuropathy, loss of vibration sense and ataxia, which belong to B12.

steps.q: Which feature most strongly suggests B12 rather than folate deficiency?
steps.r: **Neurological** signs (neuropathy, loss of vibration sense, ataxia) occur in B12 deficiency, not folate. The rest occur in both.

steps.lead: Anaemia **plus neurology** = **B12** until proven otherwise. Folate deficiency alone gives anaemia without neurological symptoms.

steps.title: B12 vs folate deficiency
head: Feature
B12 deficiency
Folate deficiency
rows: Pernicious anaemia, vegan diet, ileal disease

steps.lead: Maureen's tingling must be treated quickly: untreated B12 deficiency can leave **permanent neurological damage**.

steps.text: Do not stop at 'folate deficiency' because the patient drinks. Any **neurological** sign in a macrocytic anaemia means you must check and treat **B12**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?': FBC shows the macrocytic anaemia, serum B12 and folate confirm the deficiency, and intrinsic factor antibodies confirm pernicious anaemia.

steps.title: Maureen's bloods
steps.text: Macrocytic anaemia with **both** B12 and folate low; thyroid well replaced.

visual.title: Mean cell volume (MCV)
visual.label: Maureen 114
visual.caption: Above 100 fL: macrocytic, so check B12 and folate.

steps.lead: Maureen's **FBC** showed the macrocytic anaemia; **B12 and folate levels** then confirmed both are deficient.

visual.title: Serum vitamin B12
visual.label: Maureen 92
visual.caption: Clearly deficient, with neurological signs: urgent treatment.

steps.q: Maureen's B12 is low and she has vitiligo. Which test confirms the cause?
steps.r: **Intrinsic factor antibodies** confirm pernicious anaemia and are highly specific. The Schilling test is no longer used.

steps.lead: Maureen's **intrinsic factor antibodies** come back positive: **pernicious anaemia**.

points: Blood film: oval macrocytes and **hypersegmented neutrophils**.
Diagnosis: pernicious anaemia, plus dietary folate deficiency.

steps.text: Hypersegmented neutrophils (6 or more lobes) mean **megaloblastic** anaemia (B12 or folate). Hyposegmented (Pelger-Huët) neutrophils mean MDS.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': B12 is replaced (IM hydroxocobalamin), folate with 5 mg oral folic acid daily, and when both are low B12 comes first.

steps.q: Maureen is low in both B12 and folate. What do you start first?
steps.r: **Treat B12 first** (or alongside). Folic acid alone could precipitate **subacute combined degeneration** of the cord.

steps.lead: Maureen starts **IM hydroxocobalamin 1 mg three times weekly**, with **5 mg folic acid** daily once B12 is under way.

steps.title: Macrocytic anaemia: treatment order
nodes: Folate low too → add 5 mg folic acid after B12 started
Folate low alone → 5 mg folic acid daily
steps.caption: B12 always before (or with) folate.

visual.title: Maureen's response to treatment
visual.caption: Hb climbs and MCV falls over weeks; a reticulocyte surge comes first, within days.

steps.lead: Pernicious anaemia means Maureen cannot absorb B12 from food: she needs **lifelong** injections. Her diet and alcohol are addressed for her folate.
Her tingling and unsteadiness are why B12 cannot wait: untreated, the **neurological damage can become permanent**.

steps.text: Never give **folic acid alone** to a patient who might be B12 deficient. The blood count improves while the cord damage gets worse.
Pernicious anaemia **predisposes to gastric carcinoma**: new dyspepsia, weight loss or iron deficiency in Maureen needs urgent endoscopy.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why both cause megaloblastic anaemia (thymidine and DNA synthesis), why only B12 causes neurology (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase), and why folic acid alone is dangerous.

steps.lead: Maureen's red cell precursors cannot make **thymidine** fast enough, so the nucleus lags behind the cytoplasm and the cells stay large.

steps.title: From missing vitamin to big red cells
nodes: Thymidine synthesis fails, DNA synthesis slows

steps.lead: Maureen's tingling comes from the second B12 reaction: **methylmalonyl-CoA mutase**. Methylmalonic acid builds up and disrupts **myelin**.

steps.r: **Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase** needs B12; its failure disrupts myelin. Folate deficiency spares this pathway, so no neurology.

steps.lead: Maureen's antibodies attack **intrinsic factor** (and the parietal cells that make it), so B12 is not absorbed however much she eats.

steps.title: Normal B12 absorption
nodes: Binds intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells
B12–intrinsic factor complex travels down the gut
steps.caption: Pernicious anaemia breaks step 2; ileal resection or Crohn's breaks step 4.

steps.lead: Folic acid alone would feed Maureen's DNA synthesis and **mask the anaemia**, while the myelin damage carried on unchecked.

mcq.q: What MCV defines a macrocytic anaemia?
What is the most important cause of B12 deficiency?
mcq.r: **Pernicious anaemia** (antibodies to intrinsic factor). Alcohol and pregnancy cause folate deficiency.

mcq.q: Which feature occurs in B12 but not folate deficiency?
mcq.r: **Neurological** signs (loss of vibration sense, neuropathy, ataxia) are B12 only.
B12 is absorbed in the **terminal ileum**, bound to intrinsic factor.
**Intrinsic factor antibodies** are the most specific test.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard test for B12 and folate deficiency?
mcq.r: Blood **B12 and folate levels** confirm it; the FBC (high MCV) prompts the test.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for folate deficiency?
o: Folic acid 5 mg orally once daily
IM folic acid three times weekly
mcq.r: **5 mg oral folic acid** once daily.

mcq.q: Both B12 and folate are low. What is treated first?
mcq.r: **B12 first**, to avoid precipitating subacute combined degeneration of the cord.

mcq.q: Which reaction explains the neurology of B12 deficiency?
mcq.r: **Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase** failure builds up methylmalonic acid and disrupts myelin.

mcq.q: Why do B12 and folate deficiency cause large red cells?
o: Impaired DNA (thymidine) synthesis delays nuclear maturation
mcq.r: Impaired **thymidine/DNA synthesis**: the nucleus matures slowly, giving megaloblasts.

technique.stem: A 58 year old woman has 4 months of fatigue and tingling in her hands and feet. She has vitiligo and takes levothyroxine. She has a smooth red tongue and reduced vibration sense at both ankles. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question with a macrocytic anaemia: B12 or folate, and why?

clues: tingling in her hands and feet
steps.x: Neurology means **B12**; vitiligo and hypothyroidism mean **autoimmune**; glossitis fits.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No alcohol history, and alcohol does not cause loss of vibration sense with glossitis like this.
Folate is normal and folate deficiency has no neurology.
Iron deficiency is microcytic.
MDS has no glossitis or neuropathy.

steps.x: **E. Pernicious anaemia.** Macrocytic + neurology + autoimmune disease.

technique.stem: A 55 year old woman has fatigue and pins and needles in her feet. She has type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease. She eats meat most days and does not drink alcohol. A blood film shows macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause?

steps.x: Confirm the cause of an already-proven B12 deficiency.

clues: pins and needles in her feet
steps.x: Low B12 despite a good diet in someone with other autoimmune disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Coeliac affects the proximal gut and causes folate and iron deficiency, not first choice here.
Marrow biopsy is not needed for megaloblastic anaemia with a clear cause.
Nerve studies describe the neuropathy but not its cause.
Ferritin assesses iron; the anaemia is macrocytic.

steps.x: **C. Intrinsic factor antibodies.** The most specific test for pernicious anaemia.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man has fatigue and unsteadiness. He drinks 40 units of alcohol a week and eats poorly. He has reduced vibration sense in both feet. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Oral folic acid 5 mg daily alone

steps.x: Initial management with two deficiencies: which comes first?
Both B12 and folate are low, with neurological signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Start **B12 (IM hydroxocobalamin)** first, then add folic acid.

elim: Folic acid alone risks subacute combined degeneration of the cord.
Iron is for microcytic anaemia.
Hb 88 in a stable patient does not need transfusion.
Thiamine matters in alcohol excess but does not treat this anaemia.

steps.x: **A. IM hydroxocobalamin.** Combined deficiency: B12 first.

technique.stem: A 32 year old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant has fatigue and breathlessness. She has had severe nausea and has eaten little for months. Neurological examination is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her raised MCV?
o: Impaired thymidine synthesis delaying nuclear maturation
Methylmalonic acid accumulation in red cells

steps.x: Mechanism of macrocytosis in folate deficiency.
Pregnancy plus poor intake: **folate** deficiency; no neurology fits.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Folate is needed for **thymidine** synthesis; DNA synthesis lags and cells stay large (megaloblastic).

elim: Haemolysis raises MCV slightly but nothing suggests it.
Methylmalonic acid explains B12 neurology, not folate macrocytosis.
Intrinsic factor loss is pernicious anaemia; her B12 is normal.
Impaired haem synthesis gives microcytosis.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman has 5 months of tiredness and a sore tongue. She has vitiligo and hypothyroidism. She has pallor, glossitis and absent vibration sense at both ankles, and Romberg's test is positive. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Macrocytic anaemia with glossitis and dorsal column signs in a woman with autoimmune disease is pernicious anaemia. Folate deficiency causes no neurology.

steps.x: Diagnosis: which cause of macrocytic anaemia?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Coeliac causes iron/folate deficiency, not this neurology.
Folate deficiency has no neurological signs.
Hypothyroidism alone does not cause glossitis with dorsal column loss; she is already treated.
Iron deficiency is microcytic and ferritin is normal.

practice.stem: A 49 year old man has 3 months of fatigue. He drinks 60 units of alcohol a week and eats mainly takeaway chips. He has pallor and glossitis. Neurological examination is normal. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Alcohol excess and poor diet with a macrocytic anaemia, low folate, normal B12 and no neurology is folate deficiency.

steps.x: Alcohol and poor diet cause **folate** deficiency; no neurology.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Spherocytosis is a haemolytic anaemia with jaundice and splenomegaly.
Iron deficiency is microcytic.
MDS would not have low folate as the explanation.
B12 is normal.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has 6 months of tiredness and numbness in both feet. She has followed a strict vegan diet for 5 years and takes no supplements. She has reduced vibration sense at both ankles. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
practice.e: B12 is found in meat and fish, so a strict vegan diet without supplements causes dietary B12 deficiency, here with neuropathy. Folate is high, as vegan diets are rich in greens.

steps.x: Cause question: why is the B12 low?
B12 comes only from animal foods; neuropathy fits B12.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Coeliac affects proximal absorption (iron, folate) more.
Folate is normal.
Hypothyroidism does not lower B12.
Pernicious anaemia is possible but less likely than the obvious diet in a 27 year old.

practice.stem: A 44 year old man with Crohn's disease had a terminal ileal resection 4 years ago. He now has fatigue and tingling in his feet. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
o: Iron deficiency from GI blood loss
Loss of the B12 absorption site
practice.e: B12 is absorbed only in the terminal ileum, so resection removes the absorption site, giving B12 deficiency with neuropathy that needs lifelong replacement.

steps.x: Cause: link the history to the low B12.
Terminal ileum = B12 absorption site; neuropathy fits B12.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Loss of the terminal ileal absorption site**.

elim: Chronic disease anaemia is normocytic or microcytic.
Bacterial overgrowth tends to raise folate, not lower it.
Iron deficiency is microcytic.
Antibodies are not needed to explain it: the ileum is gone.

steps.x: **D. Loss of the absorption site.** Lifelong B12 after ileal resection.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman has 3 months of fatigue and tingling in her feet. She has a smooth red tongue. She has pernicious anaemia diagnosed today, with a haemoglobin of 87 g/L and MCV of 114 fL.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on neurological examination?
o: Loss of vibration sense in the feet
practice.e: B12 deficiency affects peripheral nerves and the dorsal columns, so loss of vibration sense in the feet is the classic finding, often with ataxia.

steps.x: Finding question: what will the neurological exam show?
B12 neuropathy and dorsal column involvement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Facial weakness is not a B12 feature.
Fasciculations are LMN signs, e.g. motor neurone disease.
Resting tremor is Parkinson's disease.
B12 affects the legs and sensation first, not isolated arm spasticity.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man with a macrocytic anaemia was started on oral folic acid by his GP 6 weeks ago without other tests. His haemoglobin has improved, but he now has worsening numbness, unsteady gait and weak legs. He has absent ankle jerks and extensor plantars. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
practice.e: Folic acid alone in an unrecognised B12 deficiency improves the blood count but lets the cord damage progress: subacute combined degeneration, with absent ankle jerks and extensor plantars.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a new neurological picture.

clues: absent ankle jerks and extensor plantars
steps.x: Folate masked B12 deficiency; mixed UMN and peripheral signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cervical myelopathy does not explain low B12 or absent ankle jerks.
GBS is acute, ascending and areflexic without extensor plantars.
MND has no sensory loss.
MS is relapsing in younger adults.

steps.x: **E. Subacute combined degeneration.** Never give folate alone before checking B12.

practice.stem: A 64 year old woman has 3 months of tiredness and breathlessness. She has pallor and a smooth tongue. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 126/74 mmHg. A full blood count has just been done.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: The FBC shows a macrocytic anaemia; serum B12 and folate levels are the gold-standard next test. Ferritin is for microcytic anaemia.

steps.x: Next investigation after a macrocytic FBC.

clues: A full blood count has just been done

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Marrow biopsy is not needed first.
Electrophoresis is for haemoglobinopathies (microcytic).
Ferritin is for microcytic anaemia.
Endoscopy comes later only if gastric symptoms.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman has a macrocytic anaemia and paraesthesia in her feet. She eats a normal diet including meat. She has autoimmune thyroid disease. Her serum B12 is 98 ng/L (200–900) and folate is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most specific test for the likely cause?
practice.e: Intrinsic factor antibodies confirm pernicious anaemia and are highly specific. Parietal cell antibodies are more sensitive but much less specific.

steps.x: 'Most specific' for the cause of B12 deficiency.
Low B12 despite a good diet, plus autoimmunity: pernicious anaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Parietal cell antibodies are sensitive but not specific.
TPO antibodies relate to her thyroid, not B12.
Methylmalonic acid confirms B12 deficiency but not its cause.
Gastrin rises in pernicious anaemia but is non-specific.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman has fatigue and paraesthesia. She lives alone and eats poorly. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. She has reduced vibration sense in both feet.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Oral folic acid 5 mg daily alone
Oral iron and review in 4 weeks
practice.e: In combined deficiency B12 is replaced first, before folate, to avoid precipitating subacute combined degeneration of the cord.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Folic acid alone can precipitate cord degeneration.
Iron treats microcytic anaemia.
She is stable; transfusion is not needed.
Diet alone is too slow with neurological signs.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman who is 26 weeks pregnant has tiredness. She has had poor appetite. Neurological examination is normal. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral folic acid 400 micrograms once weekly
Oral folic acid 5 mg once daily
practice.e: Isolated folate deficiency with a normal B12 is treated with 5 mg oral folic acid once daily.

steps.x: Pregnancy causes folate deficiency; B12 normal, no neurology.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Hb 95 does not need transfusion.
B12 is normal.
Iron treats microcytic anaemia.
That dose and frequency are too low to treat deficiency.

practice.stem: A 39 year old man had a terminal ileal resection and ileostomy for Crohn's disease. His B12 deficiency has been corrected with a loading course of injections. His haemoglobin is now 138 g/L and MCV 91 fL.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
o: Dietary advice to eat more meat
Repeat loading course only if symptoms recur
practice.e: With the terminal ileal absorption site lost, B12 cannot be absorbed from food, so lifelong supplementation (e.g. hydroxocobalamin every 3 months) is needed.

steps.x: The absorption site is gone permanently.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: He cannot absorb dietary B12 without a terminal ileum.
Deficiency will recur.
Folate is not the problem.
Waiting for symptoms risks permanent nerve damage.

practice.stem: A 60 year old woman has pernicious anaemia with paraesthesia and loss of vibration sense in her feet. Her serum folate is normal. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her neurological symptoms?
o: Accumulation of methylmalonic acid disrupting myelin synthesis
Impaired thymidine synthesis in Schwann cells
practice.e: B12 is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; deficiency builds up methylmalonic acid, which disrupts myelin, causing neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration. Folate deficiency spares this pathway.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Antibodies in pernicious anaemia target intrinsic factor, not myelin.
Thymidine failure explains the anaemia, not the neurology.
DHFR is inhibited by methotrexate.
Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke's and beriberi.

prompts.q: What is B12/folate deficiency and what does the blood count show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the mechanism and the MCV cut-off.

points.p: Impairs DNA synthesis
points.why: Both vitamins are needed to make thymidine.

points.p: Macrocytic (megaloblastic) anaemia
MCV above 100

prompts.q: What causes B12 deficiency and what causes folate deficiency?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the history in the stem tells you which.

points.p: B12: pernicious anaemia (most important)
B12: vegan diet, malabsorption (terminal ileum disease)
points.why: B12 is in meat and fish and absorbed in the terminal ileum.

points.p: Folate: poor diet, alcohol excess
Folate: pregnancy, malabsorption

prompts.q: What is pernicious anaemia, who gets it and what risk does it carry?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: spot the autoimmune clues in the stem.

points.p: Antibodies against intrinsic factor
Middle-aged/older women
Linked to autoimmune disease, e.g. vitiligo, hypothyroidism
Predisposes to gastric carcinoma

prompts.q: How do B12 and folate deficiency present, and which features tell them apart?

points.p: Both: fatigue, breathlessness, pallor, glossitis
B12 only: peripheral neuropathy, paraesthesia
B12 only: loss of vibration sense, ataxia

prompts.q: What is the main complication of untreated B12 deficiency?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: this is why the treatment is urgent.

points.p: Permanent neurological damage
points.why: Including subacute combined degeneration of the cord.

points.p: Ongoing anaemia and fatigue

prompts.q: How do you investigate a suspected B12 or folate deficiency?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: first-line, gold standard, then the cause.

points.p: FBC: macrocytic anaemia (first-line)
Gold standard: serum B12 and folate levels
Intrinsic factor antibodies confirm pernicious anaemia
points.why: Most specific test for the cause.

prompts.q: What is the treatment for B12 deficiency, folate deficiency and combined deficiency?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: doses and the order.

points.p: B12: 1 mg cyanocobalamin or IM hydroxocobalamin, three times weekly initially
Folate: 5 mg oral folic acid once daily
Combined: treat B12 first, before folate
points.why: Avoids precipitating subacute combined degeneration of the cord.

prompts.q: How is B12 deficiency managed long-term?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: is the absorption problem permanent?

points.p: Lifelong supplementation if terminal ileal absorption is lost (e.g. ileostomy)
Treat the underlying cause: diet, malabsorption, autoimmune disease

prompts.q: Why do B12 and folate deficiency cause megaloblastic anaemia, and why does only B12 cause neurology?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two reactions, two consequences.

points.p: Both are cofactors for thymidine (DNA) synthesis via the folate cycle
Nuclear maturation lags, giving large megaloblastic red cells
B12 is needed for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
Methylmalonic acid accumulates and disrupts myelin

prompts.q: Why does pernicious anaemia cause B12 deficiency, and why is folic acid alone dangerous?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: absorption, then the masking problem.

points.p: Antibodies target intrinsic factor or the parietal cells that make it
points.why: B12 not absorbed despite adequate intake.

points.p: Folic acid alone masks the anaemia
points.why: It fuels DNA synthesis via the folate pathway.

points.p: Neurological damage progresses unchecked

glossary.Macrocytic: Red cells larger than normal, with an MCV above 100 fL.
glossary.Megaloblastic: Anaemia with large, immature red cell precursors caused by impaired DNA synthesis (B12 or folate).
glossary.Megaloblasts: Large red cell precursors whose nucleus matures more slowly than the cytoplasm.
glossary.MCV: Mean cell volume: the average size of red cells; above 100 fL is macrocytic.
glossary.Pernicious anaemia: Autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor, so vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed.
glossary.Intrinsic factor: A protein from gastric parietal cells that binds B12 so it can be absorbed in the terminal ileum.
glossary.Parietal cells: Stomach lining cells that make acid and intrinsic factor.
glossary.Terminal ileum: The last part of the small bowel, where B12 is absorbed.
glossary.Cyanocobalamin: A form of vitamin B12 used as a supplement.
glossary.Hydroxocobalamin: The form of vitamin B12 given by intramuscular injection in the UK.
glossary.Folic acid: Synthetic folate; 5 mg daily treats folate deficiency.
glossary.Folate: A B vitamin needed for DNA synthesis, found in leafy greens.
glossary.Glossitis: A smooth, red, sore tongue, seen in B12, folate and iron deficiency.
glossary.Peripheral neuropathy: Damage to peripheral nerves causing numbness and tingling, usually starting in the feet.
glossary.Ataxia: Unsteadiness and poor coordination; in B12 deficiency from loss of position sense.
glossary.Vibration sense: Feeling a tuning fork on bone; carried in the dorsal columns and lost early in B12 deficiency.
glossary.Romberg: A test where the patient sways or falls with eyes shut, showing loss of position sense.
glossary.Dorsal columns: Spinal cord tracts carrying vibration and position sense.
glossary.Subacute combined degeneration: B12-related damage to the dorsal and lateral columns of the cord, causing sensory loss and weakness.
glossary.Extensor plantars: Upgoing toes on stroking the sole; an upper motor neurone sign.
glossary.Hypersegmented neutrophils: Neutrophils with six or more nuclear lobes; a sign of megaloblastic anaemia.
glossary.Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase: A B12-dependent enzyme; its failure builds up methylmalonic acid and harms myelin.
glossary.Methylmalonic acid: A metabolite that rises in B12 deficiency and disrupts myelin synthesis.
glossary.Thymidine: A DNA building block whose synthesis needs folate (and B12 to recycle folate).
glossary.Tetrahydrofolate: The active form of folate used to make DNA bases.
glossary.Myelin: The insulating sheath around nerve fibres.
glossary.Vitiligo: Autoimmune loss of skin pigment; a clue to pernicious anaemia.
glossary.Ileostomy: An opening of the ileum onto the abdominal wall, often after bowel resection.
glossary.Gastric carcinoma: Stomach cancer; pernicious anaemia raises the risk.
glossary.Reticulocyte: A young red cell; the count rises within days of starting B12.
glossary.Anti-parietal cell antibodies: Antibodies found in pernicious anaemia; sensitive but less specific than intrinsic factor antibodies.
glossary.Schilling test: An old test of B12 absorption, no longer used.
glossary.Pelger-Huët: Hyposegmented neutrophils seen in myelodysplastic syndrome, the opposite of hypersegmentation.
glossary.Thiamine: Vitamin B1; deficiency in alcohol excess causes Wernicke's encephalopathy.
